newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER PUTS TRACK ROW BEHIND HIM.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER PUTS TRACK ROW BEHIND HIM.

text.p: Double world Formula One champion Michael Schumacher "agreed to disagree" with Australian Grand Prix chief Ron Walker on Thursday after a public row about the track for this weekend's season-opening race.

Earlier this week Walker described Schumacher as a "flash in the pan" and an "overpaid prima donna" after the driver had said the Albert Park track was "nothing special" and needed improving in a few places.
Encouraged by Formula One supremo Bernie Ecclestone, the two men met on Thursday morning to settle their differences.
Walker, pilloried by the Australian media for the nature of his attack on Schumacher in the Melbourne press, said he had held a long meeting with him to discuss the problem.
"I have great respect for Michael and I am delighted the track was certified last night," he said. "It is one of the safest and the best tracks in the world."
"Mr Schumacher and I had long talks with (Ferrari team manager Jean) Todt and Mr Ecclestone about the track," said Walker. "We agreed to disagree on some areas."

Walker said that some of the adjustments made to improve the track this year fell in with the ideas put forward by Schumacher, whose comments were much less critical than originally presented by a local newspaper on MOnday.
At the news conference, copies of Schumacher's orginal comments -- as made in a survey sent out to all drivers -- were handed out.

These showed that in answer to a question asking him to rank the track, Schumacher said: "There is nothing special with this track. It is not very demanding for the driver. It does not have real fast corners."

Asked how it could be improved, he said: "Safety could be improved. There are some places which could be optimised. And it would be helpful to think about creating better possibilities to make passing other cars more easy.
"Slow corners at the beginning and the end of the straights could help to pass under braking."
Schumacher made it clear he was not impressed with the way in which his comments had been handled by the paper, but denied that the media-hyped furore would affect his concentration this weekend.
"Being chased by photographers, I suppose this is the life of a Formula One driver."
